results.title: Protocol - Baseline Soil Sampling and Analysis- GLBRC Intensive Site
results.content: HOME > PROTOCOLS > BASELINE SOIL SAMPLING AND ANALYSIS- GLBRC INTENSIVE SITE. ### Fall Surface Soil Sampling. Fall surface soils samples are taken to 25 cm in two depth increments: 0-10 and 10-25 cm using an 8 cm dia. Soils at stations are composited by depth, to yield 3 composite samples per plot for each depth increment. Back in the lab, soils are weighed, sieved, and subsampled to provide the following measures: bulk density, total carbon and nitrogen, inorganic nitrogen, pH, gravimetric moisture, and microbial biomass. A separate 0-25 cm subsample taken by push probe and composited by plot is also sent to a university test lab for standard agronomic soil recommendations (N, P, and major cations). ### Spring Surface Soil Sampling. Spring surface soil samples are taken with a push probe (2 cm dia.) to 25 cm depth. Soils at stations are composited to yield 1 composite sample per plot. ### Deep Soil Sampling. Soil cores to 1 m depth are taken once every 5 years to follow long-term carbon change. Intact cores (6 cm dia.) are taken with a hydraulic probe (Geoprobe model RS60, Geoprobe Systems; Salina, Kansas) at each of 3 sampling stations (one core/station) in late spring / early summer. Analyses include depth to major soil horizons (Ap, Bt, and Bt2 at KBS) and by specific depth intervals (0-10, 10-25, 25-50, and 50-100 cm), bulk density, organic carbon, total nitrogen, and carbonate content. The initial sampling also includes cation exchange capacity and soil texture for each depth interval composited by plot. Follow LTER protocol: KBS026-prot01, V1 taking into consideration differences in soil core diameters and depth increments. Follow LTER protocol: KBS000 V1 after compositing soils by plot. Composite samples by plot (25 gm) and depth increment are sent to Soil and Plant Nutrient Laboratory), Department of Crop and Soil Science, Michigan State University, East Lansing. For annual fall sampling: Remaining soil after subsampling is dried and placed in 1 quart Mason jars after compositing by plot. Jars are labeled with sample date , treatment code as T-R-S where T = Treatment #, R = Replicate #, S = Station # and depth (0-10 cm, 10-25 cm, 25-50 cm and 50-100 cm).

results.title: Soil Sampling: Random, Grid, and Zone-Based
results.content: ## What Is Soil Sampling? Overall, the key goals of soil sampling are clear: fertility assessment (to guide fertilization), contamination detection (to ensure safety), research, and planning construction or land use. For instance, zone sampling (a precision-agriculture method) uses layers of data – soil type, past yields, management history – to split a field into zones of similar fertility. Key tools for planning include field maps or GPS units to mark sample spots, plus any records of previous soil tests or land use. Soil probes and augers** are the core tools for sampling. (Plastic is preferred especially if you’re testing for elements like zinc, which metal can contaminate.) Each new sample zone needs its own bucket – do not mix buckets between fields or locations. ## Soil Sampling Techniques According to 2025 global agriculture reports, zone sampling is now used on over 60% of large farms, while grid sampling is preferred for high-resolution soil fertility maps. Consistent sampling depths and good patterns can improve soil test reliability by over 40%. Zone sampling uses existing knowledge – like soil maps or yield data – to draw boundaries. Take the composite subsample for the lab.** From the well-mixed bucket, scoop out the recommended amount of soil (often 1–2 pounds or about 0.5–1 kg) into a labeled sample bag. Related:  Printed Soil Sensors Could Help Farmers Boost Crop Yields and Cut Costs Label each sample immediately.** Every bag should be clearly marked with an ID number or code, GPS location or field name, depth of sampling, and date. Always use clean gloves when handling soil after extraction – this prevents oils or chemicals from contaminating the sample. A good record might read: “Sample 5: Cornfield Zone A, sandy loam with manure history, sampled 0–6″ depth, Aug 3, 2025, composite of 12 cores.” If the samples are for regulatory or compliance testing (such as EPA soil tests), use a chain-of-custody form. ## Common Errors to Avoid During Soil Sampling According to field research in 2024, incorrect sampling depth and tool contamination are the two most common errors in soil sampling, together accounting for nearly 60% of test inaccuracies.

results.content: # Soil Sampling. Soil sampling is defined as the process of collecting soil samples from various discrete sites within a specific area and depth, which is crucial for analyzing soil characteristics and addressing research questions. ## SOIL AND VADOSE ZONE SAMPLING. Shallow soil sampling may be acquired to obtain and measure geotechnical properties below the seabed. For soil sampling, seven grids (10×10 m2) were laid randomly on both the study sites. Soil samples were excavated from different depths up to 100 cm in both the sites. These samples were analyzed for soil nutrients in the laboratory. Compared to conventional sampling, EMI is a non-invasive, relatively quick, easy-to-use, cost-effective and data-rich measure of soil variability (Doolittle and Brevik, 2014). Each commercial sensor has operational advantages and disadvantages depending on the depths and soil properties of interest, the preferred data collection mode, and soil condition at the time of sampling (Sudduth et al., 2003). Biological analyses are performed as soon as possible after soil sampling to minimize the effects of storage on soil microbial communities. If longer storage periods are necessary, the samples taken to measure most soil physiological properties (soil microbial biomass, enzyme activities, etc.) can be stored at -20 °C. Observations on a stored sample may not be representative of the undisturbed field soil. ### Soil sampling. If the physical properties of soils are of interest, e.g., bulk density, aggregate stability, water-retention characteristics, and hydraulic conductivity, then other sampling techniques are required (e.g., undisturbed cores or samples of known volume) that are best discussed with the appropriate specialists. Sampling water for subsequent microbial analysis is somewhat easier than sampling soils for a variety of reasons. First, because water tends to be more homogeneous than soils, there is less point-to-point variability between two samples collected within the same vicinity. Microbial populations in water samples change much more rapidly than those in soil samples.

results.content: Specific Sampling Procedures Plowed Field Soils Samples should be taken to the plow depth. This does not ordinarily pose a serious problem because sampling to depths of 8 to 12 inches usually results in lower soil test readings and high fertilizer recommendations. For peach and apple orchards, a sampling depth of 12 to 14 inches is recommended. Gardens The recommended sampling depth for gardens is 6 inches.
